canonical_statement: The review aimed to synthesize conceptual, methodological, regulatory, and practical considerations for evaluating predictive clinical AI and to propose a unified decision pathway linking monitoring, evidence generation, causal estimands, and model-update governance.

The authors drew on established AI reporting guidelines, recent FDA and EU regulatory frameworks, implementation research, influential clinical studies, and scoping reviews rather than describing a systematic-review search and selection process.

The review defines predictive AI as algorithms that generate risk scores or outcome predictions from clinical data and distinguishes it from generative AI whose primary function is content generation.

Performance monitoring is defined as continuous operational surveillance of deployed-model technical characteristics including calibration, discrimination, data drift, alert burden, subgroup fairness, and workflow fidelity.

Clinical impact monitoring is defined as observational prospective surveillance of clinical and fairness outcomes among patients exposed to the deployed model; it can detect whether apparent benefit persists but cannot establish causal attribution without a counterfactual comparator.

Scientific evidence generation is defined as formal investigation using pragmatic or adaptive trial designs and causal-inference techniques to estimate causal effects of AI deployment on patient outcomes.

Performance monitoring, clinical impact monitoring, and scientific evidence generation answer different inferential questions and cannot substitute for one another when causal attribution is required.

Existing quality-improvement and reporting frameworks address monitoring and trial conduct separately but do not fully specify decision rules linking operational signals to formal re-evaluation, causal estimands, and trial-design choice.

The framework is designed for predictive AI; the authors state that large language models require additional evaluation approaches because stochastic free-text outputs and evolving behavior create distinct specification and equity challenges.
Table 1 maps SPIRIT-AI, CONSORT-AI, DECIDE-AI, TRIPOD+AI, PROBAST+AI, and STARD-AI to different clinical-AI lifecycle stages and reporting or appraisal purposes.
Static randomized controlled trials may become obsolete before completion because clinical AI models and their data environments can change during lengthy trial timelines.
Changes in clinical definitions or standards of care during an AI trial can alter the target phenotype, control condition, or outcome definition and confound interpretation of a fixed trial.
Fixed trials are poorly matched to AI systems that recalibrate or learn from continuously changing data streams.

AI deployment can create performative-prediction feedback loops in which model outputs change clinician actions, future patient trajectories, and subsequent training data, undermining intervention-stability assumptions.

AI treatment effects and performance are highly context dependent on patient mix, data collection, workflows, and local practice, so results from one site or set of sites may not transport reliably to other settings.
Human-AI systems should be designed and evaluated locally and repeatedly because workflows and clinician behavior can change after AI integration.
Trials that compare AI with clinicians can miss automation bias and other interaction effects that arise when clinicians use AI recommendations in practice.
Real-world effectiveness can fail because of sociotechnical last-mile factors such as user trust, hardware constraints, connectivity, and workflow integration even when model accuracy is high.

Adaptive platform trials use a master protocol with prespecified interim rules that can add, remove, or modify intervention arms while updating randomization, sample size, or eligibility as data accumulate.

Adaptive platform architecture is well matched to iterative clinical AI because new model versions can be introduced as arms, obsolete versions retired, and safety signals repeatedly assessed across prespecified subgroups.

Clinical AI trials should include an update-governance plan specifying permissible model changes, version control and audit trails, pre- and post-update validation, pause or rollback criteria, and responsible stakeholders.

The proposed AI quality-improvement oversight team includes a clinical domain expert, data scientist or ML engineer, biostatistician or clinical epidemiologist, regulatory specialist, and patient or community representative.

Table 2 operationalizes governance through predetermined change boundaries, version control, pre-deployment validation, post-deployment monitoring, pause or rollback criteria, multidisciplinary oversight, and regulatory alignment.

For subgroup-specific drift or harm signals, the framework prioritizes pausing AI for the affected subgroup, returning that subgroup to standard care, retraining and validating the model, and redeploying only after safety checks.

Figure 1 proposes a five-phase lifecycle: development and retrospective validation; feasibility and workflow integration; preliminary efficacy and safety; pragmatic multicenter randomized evaluation; and post-deployment performance plus clinical-impact monitoring.

Low-risk externally validated models with stable operating characteristics may move from feasibility directly to post-deployment monitoring, whereas novel or high-risk AI is directed through preliminary and pragmatic trial phases before deployment.

The illustrative governance cycle for detected drift is pause the affected subgroup, perform root-cause analysis, implement a bounded update, validate the new version including fairness and silent-mode checks, then redeploy with post-update monitoring.

The proposed lifecycle supports three coexisting evidence pathways: pre-deployment trials for novel or high-risk models, monitoring-only deployment for selected low-risk externally validated models, and post-deployment escalation to formal evaluation when a monitoring signal requires causal interpretation.

Monitoring-only deployment should not be treated as a substitute for scientific evidence generation and should be limited to low-risk, externally validated, stable models and appropriate workflow or human-AI studies.

In the post-deployment escalation pathway, monitoring signals are classified as clinical outcome alerts, performance degradation, fairness violations, or context shifts and compared with prespecified thresholds.
If a post-deployment signal remains below its prespecified threshold, the framework calls for continued surveillance without escalation to formal evidence generation.

If a monitoring threshold is exceeded, the framework calls for immediate governance action such as pause or rollback for the affected subgroup plus root-cause analysis before selecting an inferential pathway.
When the problem is whether the governance process functioned as intended, the escalation pathway directs an implementation audit rather than an effectiveness trial.

When both restored model performance and continued patient benefit need to be re-established, the framework recommends a hybrid dual-primary design such as a stepped-wedge cluster randomized trial with implementation fidelity and patient-outcome endpoints.
When fundamental clinical effectiveness is in question, the framework recommends pausing deployment and initiating an effectiveness trial before re-deployment.

Evidence generated after escalation should update governance parameters such as monitoring thresholds, permitted change boundaries, and training procedures, then feed back into post-deployment monitoring.

Calibration drift within prespecified bounds and without measurable patient-outcome impact can remain under clinical monitoring, whereas performance degradation with plausible patient impact warrants formal re-evaluation.

A major failure or external context shift that fundamentally changes the clinical environment should prompt pausing the system and conducting a full patient-outcome effectiveness trial before redeployment.

Operational governance outcomes such as deployment fidelity, version compliance, and alert-burden management are necessary preconditions for safe use but do not substitute for clinical-impact monitoring or formal evidence of patient benefit.

Pragmatic trials evaluate interventions under real-world conditions with diverse populations and heterogeneous care settings, making them suitable for AI effects that depend on workflow and local human-technology interaction.

A stepped-wedge cluster randomized trial begins all sites in control and switches sites to the intervention at randomized intervals, enabling longitudinal within-site and concurrent between-site comparisons while accounting for temporal trends.

Table 3 identifies four AI-specific causal-inference problems: time-varying treatment-confounder feedback, model-version instability, underidentified subgroup effects, and failure to transport trial effects to target deployment sites.

For time-varying treatment-confounder feedback created by AI-triggered clinical actions, the review proposes marginal structural models with inverse probability weighting to estimate effects under sustained AI-guided strategies.

For mid-evaluation model-version changes, the review proposes the parametric g-formula to simulate counterfactual outcomes under alternative versioning regimes while prespecifying how the update is handled as an intercurrent event.

For clinically important underrepresented subgroups with inadequate trial sample size, the review proposes data fusion across randomized and observational sources under a shared causal model to estimate subgroup-specific effects.

For target-site generalizability failures, the review proposes transportability analysis that reweights trial estimates using the target site covariate distribution to estimate local deployment effects under explicit assumptions.

Synthetic cohorts, digital twins, and in-silico simulations can support power planning, drift scenarios, edge-case testing, and regression testing after model updates but should not replace prospective evaluation of clinical endpoints in real patients.

Clinical AI development and evaluation should be transparent about training data and curation, involve patients and advocates early, and explicitly consider marginalized communities and power dynamics.

Institutions deploying clinical AI should support clinician education through simulation-based drift scenarios, real-time model-health dashboards, and retrospective case libraries that analyze prediction errors in context.

Clinicians need calibration literacy, distributional reasoning, and structured override judgment to recognize when aggregate model performance may not apply to an individual patient and to resist automation bias.

AI should augment rather than replace human oversight because social, epistemic, commercial, geopolitical, and other determinants can produce unmeasured confounding and spurious associations that models cannot reliably anticipate.

Clinical AI evaluation should shift emphasis from narrow discrimination metrics such as AUC toward patient-centered and clinician-centered outcomes, workflow improvement, false-alarm burden, and other measures of clinical utility.

Table 4 provides a seven-step operationalization playbook covering stakeholder context, workflow integration, meaningful endpoints, prespecified update protocols, de-implementation triggers, equity checks, and holistic monitoring.

The review concludes that predictive clinical AI should be evaluated through adaptive trial designs, continuous post-deployment monitoring, explicit update governance, and patient- and workflow-centered outcomes rather than technical accuracy alone.

The proposed framework integrates performance monitoring, clinical impact monitoring, hybrid evidence generation, causal estimands, and model-update governance into one lifecycle in which post-deployment surveillance can trigger rigorous re-evaluation.

The authors recommend continued clinician involvement in AI design and monitoring, pragmatic and adaptive approaches for trialists, and lifecycle-based regulation with transparent model-change reporting and consistent post-market monitoring.
